speaker: jeff
text: Mr. Gum. Good evening, Mr. Mayor, members of the council. Tonight, I wanted to present to you a resolution for the 2019 annual action plan amendment. Also included in that is an amendment to the citizens participation plan for community development block grant and home funds and seeking council input on our economic development proposal, which is what we intend to amend the 2019 plan for. So I guess give you guys a little bit of background. It's a little bit of a different year than we're used to this year. Typically we come to you all once a year and do an annual action plan and go through that process. This year, we've got a couple of different concurrent processes going. So we've got what's before you tonight, which is the 2019 annual action plan amendment. So we're basically going in and changing the existing annual action plan, which we're working under. It expires in June of this coming year, in June 30th. The other process that we have going is what we've seen recently is the five-year consolidated plan. So you've got the 2020 to 24 consolidated plan going as well. So there's a couple of things going. It's unfortunate that we have the CDBG COVID need that we have with our community, but it does complicate things and hopefully we'll get through them and I can bring clarity to both processes. So as I mentioned tonight, I wanted to discuss the 2019 amendment. The proposal before you, there's a couple of different options, option one and option two. The proposal would be to fund $350,611 that the city is receiving as part of the CARES Act for COVID-19 businesses that are impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic. So the original time that we came, I'm trying to remember the date, April 13th. So we did come back to council April 13th. Mr. Buehler and myself discussed some of the CARES Act funding that we had seen coming down the pipe. There isn't really a lot of clarity in the CARES funding. There's still some ambiguity from HUD. We have not seen an actual funding letter. We've seen funding amounts. We haven't seen any dates in there. There's been a little bit of, I don't know, we've had some followup with HUD staff and even HUD staff is a little bit unsure as to when these funds are actually going to hit localities. So we're all kind of working on the same moving target going forward. So what I wanted to bring to you tonight is kind of the proposal and some of the staff research that we had done to develop the business loan program. So what we would be proposing would be a small business emergency assistance program. And again, that would be the 300 and roughly $51,000. Of those funds, $325,611 would be used to fund either a loan or a grant program. And the $25,000 of those funds would be used to fund an administration pool to manage that program. The administration pool would basically cover things like marketing, program monitoring, publishing, some things that we have to get out to the sub-recipients that would be receiving these funds as businesses. The other thing is when we do loan monies or grant monies to businesses or anyone, there's some admin time that goes into monitoring from a CDBG perspective. And our monitoring would be specific to jobs created or jobs retained. So when we loan monies, the CDBG goal is a low-income individual benefiting through job retention in this case. So there's some follow-up after loans are made to ensure that the businesses are in fact retaining jobs for individuals. The timelines that we're looking at, this is kind of an expedited process. This annual action plan amendment for 2019, HUD allowed a number of waivers. When the CARES funding came through about a month ago, HUD realized in order to get these funds out as quickly as they could, they couldn't follow their old rules. So amazingly enough, HUD kind of got a little bit ahead of themselves, which was a good thing. Relieved a little bit of the red tape and some of the processes. So this process specifically has a five-day comment period versus a typical 30-day comment period. And then it released some of the issues with the whole public meetings and some of that. So it's a much more streamlined process to get the funds out. That being said, unfortunately, we still don't know when we're gonna get the funds. We are operating on a May 15th, somewhere in that ballpark deadline is what HUD is proposing that they will get us some of the timelines and some of the expenditures to us. So the proposal that, again, that we're looking for would fund businesses up to $10,000. The businesses would have 10 or fewer employees. The assistance could be, we're proposing option one would be a loan. It would be a 0%, no interest deferred loan for payments. Sorry, payments deferred up to 12 months. Businesses that would be assisted, we would tie the assistance to a number of employees. So what we were proposing is a $2,500 loan per employee. So depending on how many employees one was applying for, you could max out at $10,000. If someone came in with two employees, they could have a $5,000 loan and so forth, up to the $10,000. The businesses would be required to have a physical location in the city of Lakewood. So it would be specific to bricks and mortar sorts of businesses to be loaning to. We would want to limit the loans to one time for a business. So if an individual had multiple businesses, multiple franchises in the city of Lakewood, we would limit them to one loan per ownership. Businesses would have to, clearly it's COVID-19 funding. So they would have to be impacted by the COVID-19 epidemic. So whether that be business closures or impacts to their bottom lines through reductions in income, those sorts of things, they would have to document that for us as well. Businesses would have to be operational for at least one year. So one plus years they would qualify. And then we would, again, we're looking at job creation, job retention, and we would do marketing for this program with a special emphasis in some of the Hispanic neighborhoods and some of the Asian neighborhoods. So we have a very strong Korean business community. We have reached out to Yehee Han and other individuals to translate this into Korean for us. Yehee was very excited to do that. She has a couple of different pipelines that she can work with. And she mentioned to us that, oops, when we do get this program running, she would be able to get that out to the community and most likely inundate the program. So we're pretty confident that we can get the information out there and translate it fairly quickly. What we intend to do would be, I believe about four or five years ago, we had a business loan program. So the loan documents are already in place. It would take staff a minimum number of hours to actually modify those loan documents, depending on how council chooses to do the program, whether it's a loan or a grant. There's still documentation that have to be done for HUD, but those are in essence done and waiting just to be modified. So it would be a fairly simple program for us to roll out. Staff with the city of Lakewood that would be involved with this would be myself, Becky Newton, the economic development manager, and Martha Larkin, the community development block grant coordinator. So we should be able to get the programs up and running fairly quickly. Tacoma, as we're doing this with a consortium with Tacoma, is looking right now to get their program up and running by May 12th, I believe. Yes, May 12th is their council meeting. The city of Tacoma is looking to do grants for individuals, for, I believe it's just households. So they're actually granting monies for income payments, basically up to three months. So Tacoma would roll their program out. We would roll our program out. And we anticipate doing that as soon as May 13th, depending on what council decides to do. Some of the programs I wanted to go out and see what was out there in the community and did a little research one afternoon. And I was kind of shocked that there was as many programs as there were out there, but about half of them looked like they were closed. So a lot of the programs that I looked at were offered by the small business administration and they're open to anybody, assuming that they were open. But a number of those were closed. You've got the Paycheck Protection Program. That program operated with a $10 million budget and it was closed in 13 days. That was a program that provided grants to businesses. It was a 75% payroll, 25% other eligible costs. And then all those programs, or all those funds in that program are expended or accounted for. So that's program is closed. There's some economic development disaster impact loans that the small business administration had or that they still have. For $10 billion, that program is closed. Again, not all of the funds are dispersed, but they're spoken for. So those funds are closed. Those did some of the same sort of things. Those provided capital grants to businesses to operate. They were fairly large scale loans up to $2 million. And most of those loans were, or at least are being given out to businesses with prior relationships with the lenders. So they're not an easy loan to get ahold of. There's some debt relief programs through the Small Business Administration that were tied to 7A loans and SBA loans and so forth. And I got a call a couple of days ago and one of our loans that we did for Section 108 Curbside Motors. When Curbside Motors moved here, he actually qualified for the debt relief program. So when we loaned a $700,000 Section 108 loan, tied to that was a 7A SBA loan. So his business is receiving six months assistance with that program, which was kind of a nice thing to hear that somebody in Lakewood is benefiting from some of these. Some of the other programs, Washington had a Working Washington Small Business loan program or as a grant program. It was a $10 million program. That program is closed and it did something along the lines that we're proposing the same sort of deal. So up to $10,000 in assistance for businesses with up to 10 employees. Pierce County has a program available right now. They've upped their loan program very recently. It's a $20,000 loan program, $1,000 per employee, 0% interest deferred for 12 months. So it's a similar program to what we would be proposing. And then there's things out there available to some of the small businesses. The things like the federal income taxes have been delayed into July. Some of the state taxes have been starting to be pushed off. So there's some programs out there that are available. The problem is, is they're very limited and many of them have already been spoken for. So there's not a lot of options for Lakewood businesses. This would be another option for the City of Lakewood. The documents that we've provided for you, I wanted to make sure that you guys were, council members were all aware of kind of what's what in front of you. So there's three specific things that were provided. We provided the citizen participation, the CDBG, man, I'm having a rough go with this thing. The citizens, man, citizen, whatever it is. The CDBG citizen participation, Community Development Block Grant and Home Investment Partnership Act citizen participation plan. There we go, missing one word, sorry. That is included for one reason. In 2000, or sorry, in the 2019 annual action plan, HUD allows us to do kind of an expedited process. In order to do the expedited process, the citizen participation plan required one update. And that update was to allow us to do a virtual public hearing and allow us to take and publish our annual action plans via the web and via social media. So Facebook and those things. In years previous to this, the only way that we were able to do this process was an actual meeting in front of individuals. We had to provide the documents, actual hard documents at the library and the city of Lakewood and those places. So the citizen participation plan allows us to do that. That's a HUD requirement. So the language that we have provided in that document is just that language. It's a process to allow us to do it virtually. The other documents that we included, there's the 2019 annual action plan amendment. It's a very large document in the agenda packet. I believe it starts at about page 103, 104, somewhere in there, and it runs about 40 pages. That is the actual 2019 annual action plan that we all approved last year. The language that is the amendment is specifically italicized and underlined. So the only thing that we're changing would be the language that's italicized and underlined. And that is language specifically adopting the economic development emergency business loan program or grant program, whatever that may be. All of the other language in there is just language that was adopted previously. It's a HUD document. So what you do is you take what was already approved, you leave it there and just keep adding to it. So you end up with one kind of bulky, cumbersome document in the end, but that's the process for amending that. And then the last thing would just be the resolution. We have to approve this. Obviously it's a HUD process. So they wanted to approve via council resolution to approve the annual action plan, the citizen participation plan, and the business loan plan, however that may go forward. So hopefully that explains the documents, the process, and what we were proposing. Option, I guess I didn't go through your option two. Option, basically what we're seeking is either supportive option one, which would be a loan program, or option two, which would be a grant program. As we discuss this, myself, staff, Mr. Buehr, and the city manager looking at kind of where we're going and what's going on in the economy, who knows what's gonna happen in the future. The thought behind the loan program was if this recession continues into the future, a loan program would allow the city to recoup those funds. We could use them in the future for the exact same loan program. We could do any other loan program that council chose. You can reuse those to assist businesses. You could reuse those to assist low-income households in any way you so chose. So it is an opportunity if the recession does continue on to recoup those funds and use them again. If you choose to use a grant program, obviously it's a grant program. There would be no repayment of funds. So those are the two options. I turn it back to you, Mr. Mayor.

text: Can you hear me? Now we can. Gotta figure out where my clicker is here. Mr. Gum, I had a few questions for you on the opportunity option one versus two, loan versus grant. text: Yes, under CDBG rules, they would have to create or retain a low income job. text: Well, if it was a loan and they had provable need with declining revenues, I assume it could go toward any worthwhile expense to keep them up and running as best we could.
